definition.text: A government measure that keeps energy prices below market levels for customers, keeps them above market levels for suppliers, or cuts their costs.

facts.text: Energy subsidies can be direct cash payments or indirect support such as tax exemptions, price controls, trade restrictions and limits on market access.
The International Renewable Energy Agency tracked some $634 billion in energy subsidies in 2020, around 70% of them for fossil fuels.
Of that 2020 total, about 20% went to renewable power, 6% to biofuels and just over 3% to nuclear.
Other forms include public research, cheap government services, demand guarantees, and failing to charge for external costs such as pollution.
Choosing to subsidize one energy source more than another can affect the environment.
Early support for solar power by the United States and Germany helped bring renewable energy to market and cut emissions worldwide.
Because energy policies are interconnected across countries, regulating subsidies at the World Trade Organization is often seen as necessary.

title: Arguments for and against energy subsidies
article: Energy subsidy#Overview of all sources of energy

definition.text: The debate over whether governments should support energy prices or producers, weighing supply security and social aims against waste and environmental harm.

facts.text: Supporters say subsidies secure domestic supply, cut air pollution, help meet climate pledges, widen access to energy for the poor and protect jobs.
Critics say fossil fuel subsidies raise consumption and waste, burden public finances and hold back cleaner technologies.
In developing countries most benefits of fossil fuel subsidies go to the richest 20% of households.
The World Bank found subsidies to large energy companies unjustified but saw a case for helping the poorest households get modern energy.

contested_note: Sources set out explicit arguments for and against energy subsidies, and reform is opposed by many who see it as governments taking something away.

definition.text: A policy that makes manufacturers responsible for the environmental costs of their products across the whole life cycle, mainly the costs of dealing with them as waste.

facts.text: The concept was first formally put forward in Sweden by Thomas Lindhqvist in a 1990 report to the Swedish environment ministry.
It uses money incentives: producers who pay end-of-life costs are pushed to design greener products.
It rests on the idea that brand owners control product design and so are best placed to cut toxicity and waste.
It can take the form of reuse, buyback or recycling programs, and producers may pay a producer responsibility organization to handle used products.
Unlike product stewardship, which shares responsibility along the chain, it puts the cost of recycling into the product price and relieves local governments.
In Germany, packaging use per person fell from 94.7 kg to 82 kg between 1991 and 1998 after EPR was adopted, a reduction of 13.4%.
A drawback is the administrative burden from rules that differ between countries and waste streams.
The deposit-refund system is described as based on the principles of extended producer responsibility.

definition.text: Waste policies that require manufacturers to take back their products at the end of their useful life, or to help pay for collection and recycling.

facts.text: They were adopted where collection of hazardous products was lacking or too costly for local governments.
They aim to encourage designs for reuse and recycling, put waste costs into product prices and promote recycling innovation.
The earliest take-back schemes began in Europe, driven by scarce landfill space and hazardous parts.

title: Extended producer responsibility for electronics

definition.text: The use of producer responsibility rules to deal with e-waste, used electronic equipment that cannot safely go out with household trash.

facts.text: E-waste contains lead, mercury, brominated flame-retardants and cadmium, which are dangerous to health and the environment.
Making producers pay for recycling may lead them to design less toxic, longer-lasting electronics, so EPR is cited as a tool against planned obsolescence.
Critics worry it could raise prices, slow innovation, or let manufacturers shred second-hand goods instead of reusing them.

contested_note: Supporters say it drives greener design while critics argue it raises costs, slows innovation and is not clearly speeding greener design.
